title: Hip Osteoarthritis
case: Case: A 64-year-old woman has 2 years of groin pain spreading to the knee, worse on stairs and getting out of the car. Passive internal rotation is much reduced on the left with pain, and FADIR reproduces her groin pain. She walks with a mild limp. X-ray shows joint space narrowing. Lumbar examination is normal.

Working diagnosis: left hip osteoarthritis. Plan: education, strengthening and aerobic exercise (water exercise if painful), a stick in the right hand, footwear and chair advice, review in 4 to 6 weeks, and discuss specialist referral if function remains poor.
qa: Why examine the hip when a patient reports only knee pain? Hip pain is often felt in the knee, so a hip cause can be missed if only the knee is examined.
Why is FADIR not a diagnostic test for OA? It is sensitive but not specific, so a positive result shows an irritable hip joint and does not name the cause.
An adolescent has knee pain and a limp. What do you do? Suspect a hip cause, check hip rotation and refer urgently for slipped capital femoral epiphysis.
After a fall, an older patient has a shortened, externally rotated leg. What now? Suspect a hip fracture and call emergency services.
Why is exercise recommended even when the hip hurts? It improves pain, strength and function for many people and avoiding movement tends to worsen weakness and stiffness [Ref - to verify].

fields.Purpose: Check for the early loss of internal rotation, a common sign of hip OA
fields.Position: Supine with the hip and knee at 90 degrees of flexion, or prone with the knee bent to 90 degrees
fields.Action: Hold the lower leg and rotate it outward so the thigh rotates inward. Measure the angle (goniometer if available) and compare with the other side; note pain and end-feel
fields.Positive: Reduced internal rotation with pain or a firm end-feel; some criteria use a value around 15 to 25 degrees or less [Ref - to verify exact cut-off]
fields.Negative: Similar movement to the other side without pain
fields.Supports: Hip joint involvement; reduced internal rotation supports OA
fields.Limits: Normal range varies between people; compare with the other side
fields.Errors: Pelvis rotating; knee position changes; not stabilising the pelvis

fields.Purpose: Check whether the hip joint is irritable in a compressed position
fields.Action: Flex the hip to about 90 degrees, then adduct and internally rotate it. Hold and note pain
fields.Positive: Reproduction of the familiar groin pain
fields.Supports: A sensitive test for intra-articular hip problems, but not specific to OA, impingement or labral tears [Ref - to verify]

fields.Position: Supine, the test foot placed on the opposite knee (flexion, abduction, external rotation)
fields.Action: Gently press the bent knee downward and the opposite pelvis down
fields.Positive: Groin pain (hip joint) or back pain near the sacroiliac joint (pelvic source). Record location
fields.Limits: Not specific; also positive with muscle and joint problems [Ref - to verify]

fields.Action: Flex and adduct the hip to about 90 degrees; apply gentle compression down the thigh and move the hip in a small arc
fields.Positive: Pain, catching or grinding in the hip

redFlags.Finding: After a fall: cannot bear weight, shortened and externally rotated leg, severe groin pain
redFlags.Immediate action: Do not move the hip; emergency services

redFlags.Finding: Hot swollen hip with fever, severe pain on any movement
Adolescent with hip, thigh or knee pain and a limp
Sudden severe groin pain, steroid use, alcohol, sickle cell
Pain with impact in a runner or older person with low bone density
Constant night pain, weight loss, cancer history
Saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change

manual.name: Hip mobilization (long-axis distraction, lateral and posterior glides)
manual.why: May give short-term pain relief and range gains when added to exercise [Ref - to verify]
manual.finding: Stiff painful hip with reduced range
manual.application: Supine, gentle grades, 30 to 60 seconds per technique

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: education and exercise. Manual therapy is an optional short-term adjunct, best combined with exercise. Do not claim that mobilization rebuilds cartilage or restores a normal joint space.

exercise.Steps: Lying with the knees bent, lift the hips
Lying on the side, lift the top leg

exercise.Exercise: Hip flexor and adductor gentle stretch
Stationary cycling, walking or water exercise
exercise.Starting dose: 10 to 20 minutes, 3 to 5 days a week

exerciseNotes: Principle: exercise and education are first-line in major guidelines [Ref - to verify]. A mix of strengthening, range of motion and aerobic activity two to three times a week is common. Aquatic exercise is a good option when weight-bearing is painful.
Symptom rule: pain during exercise of up to about 4 out of 10 that settles within 24 hours is generally acceptable [Ref - to verify]. A hot, swollen hip or a sudden severe pain is not.

Weight management and aids: if overweight, modest weight loss may reduce pain [Ref - to verify]. A walking stick held in the hand opposite the painful hip reduces load. Supportive shoes, a raised chair and a raised toilet seat can help function.
modalityNotes: Medical options (decided by doctors): pain medication, corticosteroid injection for short-term relief, and total hip replacement for severe, persistent cases, which generally gives good results [Ref - to verify]. Rehabilitation before and after surgery follows the surgeon's protocol.
pathway: Any emergency or urgent flag? Yes: act as in Section G.

Age 45 or over, activity-related groin or front hip pain, reduced internal rotation and flexion, no flags? Yes: working diagnosis is hip OA; imaging can confirm and is considered by a doctor when it will change management [Ref - to verify].
Lumbar or knee source more likely? Use that pathway.
Start education, exercise and function-based treatment.
If severe pain, major loss of function or no improvement after good non-surgical care: specialist review for injection or hip replacement.
Visit 1: screen flags and the lumbar spine and knee, confirm the clinical diagnosis, explain OA in plain language, set a goal.
Early: reduce painful loading, start gentle range and strengthening, add aerobic activity.
Middle: progress strength and function; address weight, aids and footwear.
